clue.text: No fan of Lenin's initial comment on Trotsky's letters?

definitions.meaning: someone opposed to Lenin's communism, a believer in private enterprise
a remark that the first, capital letter of the name Trotsky is a T

explanation.surface: A question about who would disapprove of Lenin's opening remark on Trotsky's correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like correspondence between revolutionaries, but here it means the letters of a name; split the answer as CAPITAL IS T to hear the comment.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in free markets and private ownership is the natural opponent of a Bolshevik such as Lenin.

clue.text: Grounds for university to withhold minimal payment for writer

indicators.note: to withhold means to keep back, so a letter is taken out of the word for grounds

parts.note: a campus is the grounds of a university
P, a penny, is the smallest payment

explanation.surface: A university's grounds are held back to deny an author a tiny fee.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert CAMUS was the French writer of The Outsider.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus was a French novelist and essayist, author of The Plague.

clue.text: To deal effectively with father I would interrupt little boy

indicators.note: interrupt means break into, so the father and I'd go into the middle of the little boy

parts.note: a putto is a cherub-like little boy in Renaissance art
pa is an informal word for father
I'd is the contraction of I would

explanation.surface: Dad breaks in on a small child to settle things firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: A putto is the chubby winged cherub of Renaissance paintings; 'interrupt' signals that father and I'd break into it.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish or stop something decisively is an idiom for dealing with it once and for all.

clue.text: Going about on the highway with Turpin not there to disturb

indicators.note: to disturb is to throw into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The highwayman Dick Turpin is absent, so it is safe to roam the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Turpin was an English highwayman, so 'highway' suggests him; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver turning a car round to face the other way in a narrow road uses this manoeuvre.

clue.text: City porter's to carry on to the end

definitions.text: to carry on to the end

parts.note: LA, Los Angeles, is a US city
porter is a dark beer, as is stout; the 's here is a link

explanation.surface: A porter in a city must keep going till the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porter' looks like a doorman but is the dark beer, close kin to stout.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure to the finish is an idiom for surviving or lasting.

clue.text: Gunman is finally brought before the beak

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word is

parts.note: beak and hooter are both slang for the nose

explanation.surface: A gunman is at last brought before a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the beak' is British slang for a magistrate, but here it is the nose, also called the hooter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fires a gun is a marksman or gunman.

clue.text: Hits back in quarrel

indicators.note: back tells us the word for hits is read from its end to its start

parts.note: taps are light hits or blows

explanation.surface: Someone hits back during a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief petty argument is a synonym for a quarrel.

clue.text: Noise from company's plant

indicators.note: noise from tells us the answer is how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: a flock is a company of sheep or birds; with 's it gives flocks

explanation.surface: A racket coming from a firm's factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'company's plant' reads as a firm's factory; the plant is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden perennial with clustered flowers is an example of a plant.

clue.text: One paper spoilt in test — you've a long way to go here

definitions.text: you've a long way to go here

indicators.note: in places the one and the spoilt paper inside the word for test

parts.note: to try is to test
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: spoilt means ruined, so the letters of paper are jumbled

explanation.surface: A ruined exam paper and a long way still to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoilt' jumbles the letters of paper (to PPERA). The definition quotes the First World War song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary'.
explanation.definitionFit: The First World War marching song says it is a long way to this Irish town.

clue.text: Common feature of The Times and The Guardian — but not Punch

definitions.text: Common feature of The Times and The Guardian — but not Punch

parts.words: Common feature of The Times and The Guardian — but not Punch
parts.note: newspapers print a daily editorial; also both titles begin with 'The', the definite article, while the magazine's name does not

explanation.surface: Something that two broadsheets share but the humour magazine lacks.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses fit: an editorial, which papers run and Punch did not, and the word 'The' heading each title.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial expressing the paper's view, and also the definite article at the start of a name.

clue.text: Sun god's found here — associated with oral legend

definitions.text: Sun god's found here — associated with oral legend

indicators.note: oral means spoken, so the word for legend is taken by how it sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: a myth is a traditional story or legend
Ra is the Egyptian sun god; with the possessive 's he gives RAS

explanation.surface: A guidebook line saying a sun god is to be found in this place, tied up with spoken legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oral' makes the legend heard rather than spelt; the Egyptian sun god Ra with his 's ends the word, and the whole clue describes the Persian god of mystery cults.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian and Roman mystery-cult deity was worshipped as a solar god, the subject of legends passed on by word of mouth.

clue.text: Where napkin goes is somewhat obscure

definitions.meaning: at a meal a napkin is laid across the top of your thighs
to cover part of something, partially hiding it

explanation.surface: Table manners: where to put your napkin is a slightly mysterious matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' looks like an adjective meaning little-known, but it is a verb: partly to cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a phrase describing the napkin's place above the knees, and a verb for partially covering something.

clue.text: One getting blame brooded about limit to self-esteem

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for brooded encloses the other pieces

parts.note: a hen that brooded sat on her eggs
a cap is an upper limit, as on spending
ego is one's sense of self-worth

explanation.surface: Someone blamed for things sat stewing over a ceiling on their self-respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is only a link; 'about' has the word for brooded wrap round the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A person made to carry the blame for others' faults is the classic fall guy.

clue.text: The South appears to lose vital forces when team invades

indicators.note: invades means goes into, so the team's letters enter the word for losing vital forces

parts.note: to die is to lose the life force
XI is eleven in Roman numerals, the size of a cricket or football side

explanation.surface: The southern side seems to wilt when the opposing team storms in.
explanation.walkthrough: XI, Roman eleven, is a common crossword stand-in for a team. DIXIE is a nickname for the southern US states.
explanation.definitionFit: Dixie is the traditional nickname for the southern states of America.

clue.text: Sat on bronco's back here?

parts.note: a rider who sat on a horse rode it

indicators.note: back of the horse's name here means its final letter, the end of the word bronco

explanation.surface: Asking where you would sit on the back of a bucking horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: RODE plus O, the last letter of bronco, and the event where riders sit on broncos.
explanation.definitionFit: At an American cowboy show riders try to stay on bucking horses.

clue.text: So treated, weren't it right initially?

definitions.text: So treated, weren't it right initially?

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of right
treated means worked over, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: An ungrammatical question about whether something was first made right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' rearranges the letters of weren't it (to EWRITTEN), placed after the initial of right; the whole clue says the letters have been redone.
explanation.definitionFit: Words that have been written again in a new form, as these letters have been.

clue.text: Supposed originator of dance craze

parts.note: folklore held that the frenzied Italian tarantella dance was caused by, or cured the effects of, the bite of a large spider

explanation.surface: Who really started a dancing fad?
explanation.walkthrough: The tarantella of southern Italy was said to be danced by victims of a spider's bite; 'craze' hints at the supposed madness.
explanation.definitionFit: The large hairy spider gave its name to the tarantella, a dance said to be triggered by its bite.

clue.text: Composer penned in without guidance, lacking experience in any form

indicators.note: penned in means enclosed, so the composer is placed inside the word for without guidance

parts.note: unled means not led or guided
Thomas Arne was the English composer of Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A composer, confined and unsupervised, has no experience of anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arne wrote Rule, Britannia!; 'penned in' puts him inside the word for unguided.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has not been taught or schooled is ignorant or uneducated.

clue.text: Swag taken by Australian liar

definitions.meaning: Australian slang for a swagman's bundle
the girl in Hilaire Belloc's cautionary verse who told such dreadful lies

explanation.surface: An Australian thief makes off with the loot and lies about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swag' is not loot but a bushman's bedroll; Belloc's poem is about a girl who told lies and was burned to death.
explanation.definitionFit: A bushman's bedroll in Australian slang, and the lying girl of Belloc's Cautionary Tales.

clue.text: Woman's diamonds, perhaps, delivered soundly with many locks on

indicators.note: delivered soundly means spoken out, so we take the words by their sound

parts.note: diamonds are a suit in cards, so a woman's diamonds could be her suit

explanation.surface: A woman's jewels are handed over safely to someone with lots of locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diamonds' looks like jewellery and 'locks' like security; they are a card suit and hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy or shaggy describes someone with lots of hair on the head or body.

clue.text: There's nothing in marble to blend with metals

indicators.note: in puts the letter for nothing inside the word for marble

parts.note: an ally is a large or prized playing marble
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Nothing is inside the marble that could be mixed with metal.
explanation.walkthrough: An ALLY (or alley) is a choice playing marble; O for nothing goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To alloy is to fuse one metal with others into a mixture.

clue.text: One formed in smelting others?

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A question about something made while smelting other things.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across smeltING OThers, and the whole clue describes a bar cast from smelted metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A block of cast metal is produced in a mould after smelting ore.

clue.text: Hot soup giving a lot of pain in the mouth

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the end is cut from the word for a mouth pain

parts.note: a gumboil is a painful abscess on the gum

explanation.surface: A spicy soup that gives you a sore mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' trims GUMBOIL by its last two letters, IL.
explanation.definitionFit: A spicy stew from Louisiana thickened with okra is a kind of hot soup.

clue.text: A fortune might be made playing this

definitions.text: A fortune might be made playing this

parts.words: A fortune might be made playing this
parts.note: reads like a gambler's tip, but the fortune is one told: a reader lays out these cards to predict the future

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fortune' suggests wealth; it is a fortune told by a reader laying out picture cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards from a divination deck are dealt by fortune-tellers to foretell a client's future.

clue.text: It can be boring to a daughter, 17

parts.note: something boring is dull or dry

explanation.surface: Something dull being said to a daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' suggests drilling, but it means tedious. The definition '17' points to the answer at 17 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree spirit from Greek myth is one kind of nymph living in the forest.

clue.text: Acrobat with twisted back was a noble mover?

explanation.walkthrough: 'twisted back' turns only the end of TUMBLER: LER becomes REL. The cart carried French nobles to the guillotine.
explanation.definitionFit: In the French Revolution aristocrats were carted to execution in this open wagon.

clue.text: Mysterious headless fish out of tin

indicators.note: out of here means outside, so the fish's letters wrap around the word for tin

explanation.walkthrough: 'headless' cuts TUNNY to UNNY, and 'out of' puts those letters outside CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weird and inexplicable is eerie or mysterious.

clue.text: There's none at its opposite corner

parts.note: no means none, as in 'no money'
the opposite of no is yes, and OK is an assent or yes

explanation.surface: Nobody is standing at the far corner.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped 'at'. NO is set beside its opposite, OK (yes), with 'at' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small recess or out-of-the-way spot is a synonym for a corner.

clue.text: Not served by Hatter, one at tea-party put to sleep (as the eccentric Oxford don had it!)

indicators.text: as the eccentric Oxford don had it

explanation.surface: An Alice-themed riddle about a tea-party guest being put to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read 'bad it' for 'had it'. Swap the first sounds of HARE BEDDED to get the answer; the swap is by sound, so the spelling differs.
